title: Memory Techniques
summary: Learn how memory works and how to study smarter: encoding, storage and retrieval, active recall, spaced repetition and the Leitner system, chunking and mnemonics, the memory palace and learning for understanding, and sleep, health and exam strategy.
audience: Students preparing for exams, adult learners and anyone who wants a sharper memory

body.p: Memory is the brain's ability to take in information, store it and bring it back when needed. Understanding how it works lets you study smarter instead of longer.

list: Encoding: taking information in. You remember what you pay attention to and think about deeply.
Storage: keeping information over time, strengthened by sleep and repeated use.
Retrieval: bringing it back. Every time you successfully recall something, the memory becomes stronger and easier to find next time.

body.p: Working memory holds what you are thinking about right now, and it is small: a classic estimate is about 7 ± 2 items (5 to 9), and newer research suggests about 4 chunks. Long-term memory is vast. The goal of learning is to move information from limited working memory into long-term memory, connected to what you already know.
Psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus found that we forget much of new information within days unless we review it. Forgetting is normal; the techniques in this course work with it rather than against it.

body.tip: Multitasking overloads working memory; study with your phone out of sight.

body.p: Re-reading notes and highlighting feel productive, but they are among the least effective study methods because they create a false sense of familiarity. Active recall means pulling information out of memory without looking, and it is one of the most powerful learning techniques research has found.

list: Close the book and write down everything you remember about a topic, then check and fill gaps.
Make flashcards with a question on one side and the answer on the other; say or write the answer before flipping.
Answer past exam papers and practice questions.
Teach the topic to someone else, or explain it aloud as if teaching (the Feynman technique).
Turn headings in your notes into questions and answer them.

body.p: Struggling to remember is not a sign of failure; that effort is what strengthens memory. Check answers immediately so you do not reinforce mistakes.

body.tip: Spend at least half of your study time testing yourself rather than reading.

body.p: Spreading reviews over time is far more effective than cramming the same total hours the night before. Each review interrupts the forgetting curve and makes the memory last longer, so reviews can be spaced further apart.

After learning something, review it after about 1 day, then 3 days, 7 days, 14 days and 30 days. These five reviews span 55 days in total and can keep information for months. Flashcard apps such as Anki use algorithms to schedule reviews automatically, showing difficult cards more often.

list: Use boxes for paper flashcards (the Leitner system): cards you get right move to a box reviewed less often; cards you get wrong move back to the first box.
Mix topics in a review session (interleaving); it feels harder but improves long-term learning and the ability to choose the right method in exams.
Plan a study calendar backwards from exam dates.

body.tip: Short daily sessions of 20 to 25 minutes beat one long weekly session; 25 minutes a day for four days is 100 minutes of well-spaced study.

body.p: Grouping items into meaningful chunks lets working memory hold more. A 10-digit phone number such as 0821234567 is hard to hold as ten digits but easy as three chunks: 082 123 4567. Experts in any field remember more because they see patterns and chunks that beginners do not.

list: Acronyms: ROYGBIV for the colours of the rainbow (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet).
Sentences: "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming" for the planets in order.
Rhymes and songs: tunes help many people remember lists and rules, from the alphabet to multiplication tables.
Visual images: create a vivid, unusual or funny picture linking the item to its meaning.
Keyword method for vocabulary: link a new word to a similar-sounding word and an image.

body.p: Mnemonics are best for lists and facts that must be memorised exactly. They work best alongside real understanding, not instead of it.

body.tip: Make your own mnemonics; ones you create yourself are usually easier to remember.

body.p: The memory palace, used since ancient times, places images of what you want to remember along a route you know well, such as your home or the walk to school. To remember a shopping list, imagine a giant loaf of bread blocking the front door, milk pouring from the kitchen tap and eggs balancing on the TV. To recall, mentally walk the route and "see" each item. Memory competitors use this method to memorise long sequences.

list: Connect new information to what you already know; ask how and why, not just what.
Use examples, diagrams and mind maps to show relationships between ideas.
Explain ideas in your own words.
Use dual coding: combine words with pictures, such as a labelled diagram of the heart.

body.p: Information that is understood and connected is easier to remember and to apply to new problems in exams.

body.tip: Start with a small memory palace of five locations and practise with a short list before using it for study.

list: Sleep: during sleep the brain consolidates memories. Teenagers generally need about 8 to 10 hours, adults about 7 to 9. All-night cramming harms recall the next day.
Exercise: physical activity improves mood, attention and memory.
Food and water: regular meals and staying hydrated help concentration.
Stress: some pressure helps, but high stress harms recall. Breathing exercises, preparation and talking to someone help.
Breaks: the Pomodoro method uses about 25 minutes of focus followed by a 5-minute break.

body.p: In the final weeks, focus on active recall and past papers rather than new notes. On the day, read questions carefully, write down key formulas or mnemonics as soon as you are allowed, and answer the questions you know first to build confidence. If you go blank, move on and return later; memories often surface once you relax.

body.tip: Plan your sleep before an exam as carefully as your study; a rested brain recalls far more.

options: Retrieving information from memory without looking
